::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**A provocative paper, on purpose.** This is a position paper in the form of a short scientific paper: a thesis, a model, a simulation, and predictions that could prove it wrong. It argues one side as strongly as I can. It follows [Review the Intent, Not the Diff](../2026-10-22-review-the-intent-not-the-diff/index.qmd), which kept review and changed its object; this paper asks whether we need the review at all. Figures are my own, drawn and simulated with the code in [figs.py](figs.py).
:::

**Abstract.** Human approval of every pull request became standard when code was written by hand, reviewers were the main check, and defects found late were expensive. I model the review gate as an investment that pays when $p \cdot d \cdot \Delta C > r$: the chance a change still carries a defect after automated checks, times the share a reviewer catches, times the late-fix cost avoided, must exceed the cost of the gate. Agentic coding shrinks the late-fix cost of most changes but not of all: harm that cannot be reverted keeps it high. The model therefore yields a rule rather than a ban: *approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else*. Watching means rules enforced in every session and a daily audit of the whole codebase. In a simulation of a team merging 40 changes a day, adding the gate on top of the audit costs about 10 engineer-hours for each day of latent defects it prevents. Without the gate, the audit leaves fewer latent defects than today's practice whenever it can see more kinds of defect than a reviewer would have caught, and finds them quickly enough. I give four predictions and a protocol to test them.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Claims

1. **The rule.** Approve what you cannot undo. Watch everything else.
2. **Why.** A gate pays only when $p \cdot d \cdot \Delta C > r$. Cheap fixes and fast rollback make $\Delta C$ small, except where harm survives a revert.
3. **Watching.** Rules every session must follow, merge on green, and a daily audit whose report drives the team's work.
4. **The condition.** Watching beats approving only if the audit reaches far enough and fast enough: $c > d \, (1 + h_{\text{users}} / h_{\text{audit}})$.
5. **The test.** Teams that adopt the rule should fail no more often and find defects sooner. If they do not, the thesis is wrong.
:::

## 1. Introduction

In the previous essay I argued that teams should review the intent rather than the diff. That still assumed a person would look at each change. Here I go further: for most changes, nobody should have to approve the pull request at all.

The usual answer is that this would end in chaos. I do not think so, and the reason is economic rather than ideological. Review is a control, and every control has a price. We paid it gladly because the gate was the cheapest place to catch a defect: minutes at review against days once it reached users.

Agentic coding changes the price on both sides. Rules can be enforced inside every session instead of at its end. A fix takes an agent minutes, and a flag can switch a change off in seconds. Making a correction is cheap now, and I believe that is what changes the whole picture. Human attention stays expensive, and the gate spends it on every change, whether or not that change needed it.

Correction is not cheap everywhere. Deleted data, leaked credentials or money sent to the wrong account cannot be taken back by a revert. That distinction gives the paper its rule: **approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else.**

## 2. Background: what review was for

**Inspections.** Formal code inspection was introduced at IBM in the 1970s as a defect-removal step [@fagan1976], justified by the claim that a defect costs one to two orders of magnitude more to fix in operation than during development [@boehm1981]. That curve shaped decades of process, although its empirical basis is thinner than its fame [@bossavit2015], and agile practice argued that frequent integration and automated tests flatten it [@beck1999].

**What modern review finds.** Lightweight, tool-based review replaced inspections in most teams [@rigby2013]. At Microsoft, developers named finding defects as their first motivation, but most review comments concerned code improvement and understanding [@bacchelli2013]; a later internal study was titled *Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs* [@czerwonka2015]. About three quarters of the issues found in review concern evolvability rather than behaviour [@mantyla2009; @beller2014]. At Google, people valued education, keeping norms, gatekeeping and accident prevention most [@sadowski2018].

**Evidence for review.** In three large open-source projects, components with low review coverage and participation had more post-release defects [@mcintosh2014], and careful reading at a controlled rate improves quality [@kemerer2009]. The largest survey-based study of delivery performance found that approval by an external body slowed delivery without reducing failed changes, and recommended lightweight peer review instead [@forsgren2018].

**Agentic review today.** The Claude Code team at Anthropic already lets low-risk changes merge without a person when automated review passes, and reports more merged changes and fewer reverts [@anthropic2026review]. The rule proposed here replaces their risk score with a simpler question, and makes no-approval the default.

## 3. A cost model of the gate

Consider one change. Let $p$ be the probability that it still carries a defect after all automated checks; $d$ the share of such defects a human reviewer catches; $\Delta C = C_{\text{late}} - C_{\text{review}}$ the cost avoided by catching a defect at review rather than later; and $r$ the full cost of the gate for one change, including the reviewer's reading, the author's waiting and the context switches on both sides. The gate pays for itself when

$$
p \, d \, \Delta C > r .
$$ {#eq-break-even}

The late cost has two parts: the work of the fix, and the harm done while the defect lives. If harm accrues at a rate $k$ and the defect is found after a time $\tau$,

$$
C_{\text{late}} \approx c_{\text{fix}} + k \, \tau .
$$ {#eq-late}

**What agents change.** Session rules can lower $p$: an agent can be made to add tests for every changed behaviour, keep coverage of changed lines above a threshold, and follow a conventions file, and checks delivered while code is written are the ones developers act on [@sadowski2018cacm]. This is not automatic, since code written with AI assistants can be less secure than code written without them [@pearce2022; @perry2023]; the simulation in §5 therefore keeps $p$ the same under every policy. Meanwhile $r$ does not fall: careful review proceeds at a few hundred lines an hour [@kemerer2009], volume rises, and waiting grows roughly as $\rho/(1-\rho)$ with reviewer utilisation $\rho$ [@kingman1961].

**The main assumption.** The term that moves most is $\Delta C$, and it rests on one assumption, which I state openly. *Assumption A: for most defects, an agent can produce a correct fix within an hour of the report, and a flag or a rollback can stop the harm within minutes.* Under A, $c_{\text{fix}}$ is small, flags cap $k$ [@humble2010], and an audit caps $\tau$. Some evidence points this way: agents resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation [@jimenez2024], and the best-performing teams studied in @forsgren2018 already restored service in under an hour. None of it measures agent-made fixes in production, so prediction H3 tests A directly.

![**Figure 2.** Schematic. The relative cost of fixing a defect against when it is found. The steep curve is the one usually cited for the 1970s; its empirical basis is disputed [@bossavit2015]. Practice flattened it [@beck1999]. The agentic curve is what Assumption A implies, not a measurement. The vertical arrow is what a review gate saves on the steep curve. Irreversible harm does not flatten.](figures/fig02.png){fig-alt="Log-scale chart of relative cost to fix, from 1x to 100x, against when the defect is found: while writing, at review, next day (audit), after a week, in production months later. A red line labelled irreversible harm: data loss, breach starts at 40x the next day and rises to about 75x. An amber arrow at review marks what a gate used to save."}

**Where the rule comes from.** Assumption A flattens the cost curve only for harm that a revert removes. When the harm persists after the code is reverted, $k\tau$ in @eq-late stays large however quickly the defect is found, and the gate still pays (position C in Figure 3). Everything else drifts below the break-even line (position B). The model does not say "never review". It says exactly where review still pays.

## 4. The rule in practice

**What cannot be undone.** A change is a one-way door [@bezos2016] when its harm survives a revert: data destroyed or exposed, money moved, credentials or signing keys changed, a public interface released to people outside the team, a message sent to customers. The list is explicit, versioned, and part of the session contract; a change that touches it waits for a person. A second case belongs to the same category. A session that has followed instructions from outside the team, such as an outsider's issue or a web page, can be steered by that content [@greshake2023], and a planted backdoor or a leaked secret cannot be undone either. Such a session's changes wait for a person too. Reading a library's documentation is data, not an instruction; what matters is whether outsiders could direct the agent.

**What watching means.** Everything else merges on green and is watched at three points (Figure 1, Table 1). Before the merge, a *session contract* that every session follows, enforced by the agent and by CI. After the merge, *flags and monitoring* in production. And once a day, an *audit* that reads the whole codebase and the production signals, not the latest diff, and writes a short report that the team reads instead of forty diffs. When the same problem keeps appearing in the report, the team turns it into a rule, so that the contract gradually absorbs what reviewers used to write in comments.

**What the audit sees that a pre-merge check cannot.** Fast checks belong in the contract. The audit is for four things a per-change check cannot do: *slow* checks such as mutation testing and fuzzing; patterns *across* changes, where two correct changes conflict or an architecture rule erodes one step at a time; *production* signals since yesterday's merges; and *trends* that people can judge before any rule encodes them. A per-change reviewer cannot see the second and third kind either.

| | Session contract (every change, blocking) | Daily audit (whole codebase, advisory) |
|---|---|---|
| Tests | Tests added or updated for each changed behaviour | Mutation score by module, and its trend |
| Coverage | Coverage of changed lines ≥ threshold; total never decreases | Untested hotspots: code that changes often and is weakly tested |
| Integrity | No test deleted or assertion weakened without a linked decision | Weakened or skipped tests, by session |
| Conventions | Conventions file, linters and types pass | Drift from conventions and architecture rules |
| Intent | A change to a contract or invariant updates its decision record | Decision records changed since yesterday |
| Production | User-facing behaviour behind a flag | Errors and performance since the last merges |
| One-way doors | Listed paths, and sessions steered from outside, wait for a person | Every change to a listed path |

: **Table 1.** A minimal session contract and audit. Thresholds and exact checks are for each team to set; the split is the point. What can be decided per change is enforced by machines; what needs judgement is batched once a day for people.

Two rules in the table close known gaps. The integrity rule stops the most common failure of coding agents, an agent that edits a test until it passes. And coverage is paired with mutation testing, because coverage alone is a weak measure of test quality [@inozemtseva2014] and becomes a target as soon as it is enforced [@strathern1997], while mutation testing measures whether tests notice a change in behaviour [@papadakis2019].

**Who is accountable.** The person who starts a session owns what it merges. Steering the agent and looking at its output is part of writing, and it stays. What disappears is the second person whose approval was required before the change could land.

**Intent changes.** In the previous essay I wrote that a change to the intent should always go to a person before it merges. The rule refines that position. A change to a contract or an invariant that can be reverted merges like any other, but never silently: it updates its decision record, and the team reads it the next morning. Only intent that guards a one-way door still waits for approval.

## 5. A simulation

I simulated a team under four policies: a gate without an audit (today's common practice), an audit without a gate (the proposal), both, and neither. The parameters (Table 2) are chosen rather than measured and, where I had to choose, generous to review.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Changes per day, $\lambda$ | 40 in Figure 4b and Table 3; 5 to 56 in Figure 4a |
| Automated checks (CI and AI review) | log-normal, mean 24 min |
| First review round | log-normal, mean 20 min, coefficient of variation 1 |
| Second round | needed by 40% of changes, after a 2 h author turnaround; mean 10 min |
| Reviewer capacity | 3 full-time equivalents, first come first served, no batching |
| Residual defect probability, $p$ | 0.05 per change, under every policy |
| Share caught by a reviewer, $d$ | 0.5 |
| Daily chance users or monitoring find a latent defect, $h_{\text{users}}$ | 0.10 |
| Daily chance the audit finds a defect it can see, $h_{\text{audit}}$ | 0.50 (varied in Figure 5) |
| Share of defects the audit can see, $c$ | 1 (varied in Figure 5) |
| Horizon | 60 working days, 300 runs |

: **Table 2.** Simulation parameters. The review queue is optimistic for the gate: reviewers start as soon as they are free. A value of $d = 0.5$ is high for functional defects given what review is known to find [@mantyla2009; @czerwonka2015].

The green line, merge on green, stays flat near 20 minutes. Right, latent defects in main over 60 working days. The red dashed line, no gate no audit (chaos), rises to about 20. The navy line, gate no audit (today), rises to about 10. The green line, no gate daily audit (proposed), stays near 3.3. The amber line, gate and daily audit, stays near 1.7."}

| Policy | Median time to merge (90th pct.) | Reviewer hours per day | Latent defects in main | Median age of a defect when found |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gate, no audit (today) | 1.1 h (4.1 h) | 16 | 9.7 | 6 days |
| No gate, daily audit (proposed) | 0.4 h (0.7 h) | about 1, reading the report | 3.3 | 1 day |
| Gate and daily audit | 1.1 h (4.1 h) | about 17 | 1.7 | 1 day |
| No gate, no audit | 0.4 h (0.7 h) | 0 | 19.5 | 6 days |

: **Table 3.** Simulation results at 40 changes a day. Latent defects are those present in main during a day, averaged over days 21 to 60. Run `python figs.py` to reproduce them.

**Chaos is real, but it is not the proposal.** Removing the gate and adding nothing doubles the latent defects of today's practice. The critics are right about that policy; they are wrong that it is the only alternative to the gate.

**The price of the gate.** Holding the audit fixed, adding the gate lowers latent defects from 3.3 to 1.7 for 16 reviewer-hours a day: about **10 engineer-hours for every day of latent defects it prevents**. That number turns @eq-break-even into a question any team can answer: does a latent defect in this part of the system cost more than 10 engineer-hours for each day it lives? For a reversible defect in an internal tool, rarely. For a payment flow, easily, and that is a one-way door.

**Speed and reach of the watch.** By Little's law [@little1961], latent defects equal the rate at which they enter times how long they stay. A gate removes at most the factor $(1-d)$, here a half; an audit shortens the stay, here by a factor of six. That is why the proposal beats today's practice in Table 3. But the audit is not equally good at everything. If it can see only a share $c$ of defects, the rest are found only by users, and the proposal beats today's practice when

$$
c > d \left(1 + \frac{h_{\text{users}}}{h_{\text{audit}}}\right).
$$ {#eq-watch}

The condition has a plain reading: *the watch must see more kinds of defect than a reviewer would have caught, and the slower it is, the more it must see.* With the values of Table 2, an audit that sees every defect must find it with a daily chance above 0.10, and an audit that finds defects within a day or two must see at least 60% of them (Figure 5). If a team's defects are mostly of a kind no machine can notice, the rule fails for that team, and @eq-watch says so before any harm is done: measure $c$ first.

## 6. Predictions and a test protocol

Speed is not a useful test, since removing a gate obviously speeds up merging. The thesis stands or falls on quality and on its assumptions. For teams that adopt the rule, compared with similar teams that keep the gate:

- **H1. No loss of stability.** Change failure rate and time to restore service [@forsgren2018] are no worse, within a margin fixed in advance.
- **H2. The watch sees far enough.** The share of defects found first by the audit or monitoring rather than by users, an estimate of $c$, exceeds the bound of @eq-watch, and the median age of a defect when found falls.
- **H3. Fixes are cheap (Assumption A).** For defects found by the audit, the median time from report to merged fix is under one working hour, and a flag or rollback contains the harm before the fix lands.
- **H4. The report is used.** At least half of the audit's findings are fixed or explicitly dismissed within a week. An audit nobody reads turns the proposal into the chaos case.

**Protocol.** A stepped-wedge design fits within an organisation: teams adopt the rule one at a time, in random order, over several months, so that every team is observed under both policies and calendar effects are controlled. One-way doors keep their approval throughout. H1 is a pre-registered non-inferiority test; H2 to H4 and lead time are secondary outcomes, measured from repository, pipeline and incident logs rather than self-reports, since teams cannot be blinded. If H1 fails, or H2 or H3 fails, the thesis is wrong for the teams studied.

## 7. Objections and limitations

**"Review demonstrably reduces defects" [@mcintosh2014].** Compared with no review, on code written by hand, yes. The relevant comparison is review against watching, which is what H1 and H2 test. The recommendation of peer review in @forsgren2018 rests on data that predate agents; extending it is an extrapolation, and I state it as one.

**"Review is how teams share knowledge" [@bacchelli2013; @sadowski2018].** It was. The replacement is deliberate: decision records, conventions and a daily report that the whole team reads. One short report read by everyone shares more than forty diffs each read by one person.

**People adapt.** Without a reviewer, authors might grow careless, or more careful because they now own the result alone. The simulation holds $p$ fixed and cannot tell; H1 measures the net effect.

**Compliance.** Some standards require custom code to be reviewed before release; PCI DSS, for example, sets conditions on who may review when the review is manual [@pcidss2022]. Whether automated review satisfies such a requirement is for auditors to decide. Where it does not, the code it covers joins the list of one-way doors.

**Loss of skill.** Automation leaves people responsible for rare, hard cases while removing the routine practice that prepares them [@bainbridge1983]. With fewer people reading code daily, teams must keep that skill on purpose: reading the audit's findings in the code, tracing incidents by hand, rotating who does it.

**Limits of the model.** It is linear and treats defects as independent. It holds $d$ constant, although reviewers tire and large changes get shallower reviews, and it ignores what reviewers learn by reviewing. The parameters are chosen, not measured, and describe one team at one rate. The direction of the result holds wherever @eq-watch holds; its magnitude does not transfer. The paper also assumes that writing code is no longer the bottleneck, and the evidence on how much AI speeds up experienced developers is mixed [@becker2025].

## 8. Conclusion

The pull request review was a good answer to a question that has changed. It was the right control while late defects were expensive and a person's reading was the main check. With agentic coding, rules run inside every session, most defects are cheap to fix the next day, and the one step that has not become faster is the person reading the diff.

I have argued that the review gate should stop being the default. What keeps a codebase healthy is how quickly defects are found and how cheaply they are undone, not whether someone looked at each change before it merged. Where harm cannot be undone, a person still decides. Where a machine cannot see, the team should measure that before it lets go.

This means giving up control of each change. In return, we can simplify our processes instead of adding layers to protect a kind of control that, in the past, was the only kind available. Approve what you cannot undo. Watch everything else.
